separate_help_return_routes.whole_line_witness: Write the definition as $`q(x)=(e^{2x}+e^{-2x})/2`$. The two inner inputs have derivatives $`2`$ and $`-2`$. Keep those multipliers attached to their exponentials before combining anything. For the value at zero, both exponential values are 1. [Return to P1](lesson.md#p1)

For a quotient-rule route use $`u=\sin x`$ and $`v=1+\cos x`$. Then $`u'=\cos x`$ and $`v'=-\sin x`$. The second term in $`u'v-uv'`$ consequently has two minus signs. After expansion, look for $`\sin^2x+\cos^2x`$. The denominator restriction comes from $`1+\cos x=0`$ in the original function. [Return to P2](lesson.md#p2)

Differentiate $`xy`$ as $`1\cdot y+xy'`$. The derivative of $`y^2`$ is $`2yy'`$. Put terms containing $`y'`$ on one side, factor out $`y'`$, then substitute the point. A tangent of slope $`m`$ through $`(1,2)`$ has equation $`y-2=m(x-1)`$. [Return to P3](lesson.md#p3)

After applying the addition identity, the numerator is $`\cos x\cos h-\sin x\sin h-\cos x`$. Group the first and last terms together. That gives one multiple of $`(\cos h-1)/h`$ and one multiple of $`\sin h/h`$. Only $`h`$ varies in the limit. [Return to P4](lesson.md#p4)

For positive $`x`$, either write $`y=e^{x\ln x}`$ or take logarithms to obtain $`\ln y=x\ln x`$. The exponent, or the right-hand side of the logarithmic equation, is a product of two varying factors. Differentiate both factors using the product rule. [Return to P5](lesson.md#p5)

(b) Call the exponent $`w=x^2\arctan x`$. Write $`B'=e^w w'`$ first. To obtain $`w'`$, the factors $`x^2`$ and $`\arctan x`$ contribute derivatives $`2x`$ and $`1/(1+x^2)`$, respectively. Do not insert $`x=1`$ before differentiating. [Return to P6](lesson.md#p6)

The ordinary cosine formula applies to $`\cos`$, a different function. It would incorrectly insert an additional negative sign if copied for $`\cosh`$. The exponential definition establishes the sign directly. [Return to P1](lesson.md#p1) · [Hint P1](hints.md#h1)

A product-rule route using $`\sin x(1+\cos x)^{-1}`$ is equally valid when it preserves the same exclusions. The important numerator sign is positive in front of $`\sin^2x`$, since subtraction multiplies the negative derivative of cosine. [Return to P2](lesson.md#p2) · [Hint P2](hints.md#h2)

This line passes through the given point and has the required gradient. Treating $`y`$ as constant in $`xy`$ would omit $`xy'`$ and give the wrong denominator. [Return to P3](lesson.md#p3) · [Hint P3](hints.md#h3)

The negative sign is inherited from the cosine addition identity. It is not supplied by memorising the derivative. The limit requires radians for the two starting facts used here. [Return to P4](lesson.md#p4) · [Hint P4](hints.md#h4)

Equivalently, differentiating $`e^{x\ln x}`$ by the chain and product rules gives the same expression. The constant-power rule assumed the exponent's derivative was zero. Here the exponent is $`x`$, whose derivative is 1, and its variation creates the $`\ln x`$ term. Substituting $`r=x`$ into a rule derived for fixed $`r`$ changes that assumption. A check only at $`x=1`$ would miss this mistake because $`\ln1=0`$; at $`x=e`$ the correct derivative is $`2e^e`$, which distinguishes it from the incorrectly substituted constant-power result $`e^e`$. [Return to P5](lesson.md#p5) · [Hint P5](hints.md#h5)

Recalling the derivative formulas and their conditions is retrieval. Constructing the nested differentiation and distinguishing the two domains in (a) applies those facts to changed expressions. A successful calculation shows that this particular route worked; it does not by itself establish long-term retention. [Return to P6](lesson.md#p6) · [Hint P6](hints.md#h6)

named_return_destinations.next_nonempty_text: P1. Approximate the positive square root of 4.08 using a tangent at the nearby base point 4. Write the input displacement, the tangent formula and the estimate. Explain why the resulting number is an approximation rather than an exact identity. A complete response connects the chosen base point and derivative to the estimate.

P2. For $`g(x)=e^{3x}/(1-2x)`$, find its linear approximation about $`x=0`$ by combining basic approximations. State a neighborhood in which the original expression is defined. Identify the small inputs used in the exponential and reciprocal expansions. A proposed calculation multiplies the two linear factors and reports its $`x^2`$ term as $`g`$'s quadratic coefficient. Explain why that coefficient is not established by this calculation. A complete response supplies the linear polynomial and the reason the extra coefficient is unreliable.

P3. For $`f(x)=\ln x`$, construct its linear and quadratic approximations about $`a=2`$ and use both to estimate $`\ln(2.04)`$. For the numerical evaluation, use $`\ln2\approx0.69314718`$. The comparison value $`\ln(2.04)\approx0.71294981`$ is supplied only for checking the estimates. Compare their absolute errors at the shown precision and explain the role of $`(x-2)^2`$ in the quadratic formula. A complete response derives the coefficients from $`f(2)`$, $`f'(2)`$, $`f''(2)`$ and interprets the comparison.

P4. Determine the limit as $`x`$ tends to 0 of $`(e^x-1-x)/x^2`$. Explain why the linear approximation alone does not determine this limit, and state an error condition that makes the quadratic approximation sufficient. A complete response identifies the surviving coefficient and justifies what happens to the omitted term after division by $`x^2`$.

P5. In the stated constant-speed, gravity-free clock model, the elapsed reference-frame time $`T'`$ and the elapsed moving-clock time $`T`$ obey $`T'/T=(1-q)^{-1/2}`$, $`q=(v/c)^2`$. Take $`v=6\ \mathrm{km/s}`$, $`c=3\times10^5\ \mathrm{km/s}`$, and $`T=86400\ \mathrm{s}`$. Estimate $`(T'-T)/T`$ and $`T'-T`$ using the term linear in $`q`$. Compute the next, quadratic-in-$`q`$ contribution to the fractional correction. Does adding that contribution change the estimate at a fractional scale of $`10^{-12}`$? State which powers of $`v/c`$ these two contributions have, and distinguish the comparison of these two terms from a bound on every omitted term. A complete response keeps the fractional ratio separate from the time interval and retains consistent units.

P6. Return later, after a break if useful, and choose how many terms you need rather than starting from a method label. Let $`H(x)=\ln(1+2x)e^{-x}`$, defined near $`x=0`$. Find its approximation through degree two, then determine the limit as $`x`$ tends to 0 of $`[H(x)-2x]/x^2`$. Identify which products contribute to the coefficient of $`x^2`$ and why discarded terms do not affect the limit. A complete response connects the chosen expansion order to the cancellation in the numerator and the divisor $`x^2`$.

P2. Fix $`b\gt 0`$. On $`[0,b]`$, let $`R_n`$ and $`L_n`$ be the right- and left-endpoint sums for $`x^2`$ on $`n`$ equal subintervals. Let $`S_n`$ use any one sample point in each of those same subintervals. The bounding-pyramid argument has established $`R_n\to b^3/3`$. Show directly from the endpoint sums that $`R_n-L_n=b^3/n`$. Use this and a bound for $`S_n`$ to explain why every such choice of sample points has the same limiting total. Target: justify sample independence; a quoted antiderivative alone does not meet the criterion.

P4. A student borrows continuously for one year, with no repayments. Time $`t`$ is the numerical number of years since the start; the borrowing rate is $`f(t)=12000t`$ dollars per year for $`0\le t\le1`$. Each borrowed portion incurs simple interest at 6% per year until $`t=1`$, with no interest on interest. Construct and evaluate an integral for the principal borrowed and an integral for the final debt. Explain each factor in the debt integrand and why charging a full year's interest on all the principal gives a different result. Would uniform borrowing at 6000 dollars per year over the same year give the same final debt? Justify the comparison through timing as well as calculation. Target: construct and interpret a weighted accumulation when the rate changes.

P5. For a later study session, try this before reopening the explanation. A tank initially holds 10 litres. Its signed net flow is $`g(t)=3-t`$ litres per minute, where $`t`$ is the numerical number of minutes after starting, for $`0\le t\le4`$. Positive flow enters the tank and negative flow leaves it; assume these are the only flows and the tank has sufficient capacity. Write a representative rectangle contribution for a short interval. Find the net change, final volume, total amount of fluid crossing the boundary in either direction, and mean net flow over the four minutes. Explain why one integral cannot represent all four requested quantities unchanged. Target: retrieve the rate-times-width construction and transfer it to a signed physical total.
